11700: When something or someone is paralyzed, they are in a state of being completely unable to move or act — not just struggling, not just slow, but genuinely frozen and non-functional. The key idea is a total or near-total loss of ability, usually caused by something powerful acting on the person or thing from the outside.
The Two Main Worlds of This Word

1. The Physical World (Body & Movement)

In its most literal sense, a person or body part is paralyzed when the muscles cannot move because the signals from the brain are interrupted or blocked — usually due to nerve damage, injury, illness, or a medical condition.

  • His legs were paralyzed after the accident, and he could no longer walk.
  • The stroke left the left side of her face paralyzed.
  • The patient's right hand was paralyzed — he couldn't grip anything.

Notice a few things:

  • The paralysis is not the person's choice. It is imposed on them.
  • The body part still exists; it simply cannot respond.
  • There is typically no sensation or voluntary control in the paralyzed area.

Paralysis can be partial (only one limb, one side of the body) or complete (the entire body from a certain point downward, as in spinal cord injuries). So when we say someone is paralyzed, it helps to specify what is paralyzed, unless the full body is implied.

2. The Figurative World (Emotions, Decisions & Systems)

This is where "paralyzed" gets enormously rich — and it's used just as often as the physical sense, maybe more so in everyday language.

When a person, organization, or system is described as paralyzed in a figurative sense, it means they are so overwhelmed, blocked, or stuck that they cannot function or move forward — even though there is nothing physically wrong with their muscles.

Paralyzed by emotion

Strong emotions — especially fear, grief, shock, or anxiety — can make a person mentally frozen. They want to act but simply cannot.

  • She stood paralyzed with fear as the dog barked and lunged toward her.
  • He was paralyzed by grief after losing his father — he couldn't even get out of bed.
  • The sudden news left the entire room paralyzed with shock.

The emotion here acts like a kind of invisible force that completely shuts a person down. It's not weakness or laziness — it's an involuntary freezing.

Paralyzed by indecision or overthinking

Sometimes a person has too many choices, too much at stake, or too much uncertainty — and instead of choosing, they end up choosing nothing. They are frozen between options.

  • She was paralyzed by indecision and missed the deadline entirely.
  • He knew he had to respond, but too many conflicting thoughts left him paralyzed.

This usage highlights that paralysis isn't always about a single overwhelming emotion. Sometimes it's the sheer complexity or weight of a situation that freezes a person.

Paralyzed systems, cities, countries, and organizations

"Paralyzed" is also used to describe non-human things — systems, places, institutions — when they have completely stopped functioning.

  • The city was paralyzed by the massive snowstorm — no buses ran, no shops opened.
  • The government was paralyzed for weeks due to deep disagreements between the two parties.
  • A cyberattack paralyzed the hospital's computer systems.

Here, "paralyzed" communicates that the normal flow of activity has been completely halted — not just slowed, but frozen.
What Makes "Paralyzed" Different from Similar Words

This is important, because learners often confuse "paralyzed" with words that seem close to it.

Paralyzed vs. Stuck

"Stuck" means you're having difficulty moving forward — there's resistance, but you might still be able to push through with effort.

"Paralyzed" is far more absolute. A paralyzed person or system is not just having difficulty — they are completely unable to act. There's no pushing through.

He was stuck on the math problem. → He was finding it hard, but still engaging with it.
He was paralyzed by the math problem. → He was so overwhelmed he couldn't even begin.

Paralyzed vs. Frozen

"Frozen" is very similar and is often used interchangeably with "paralyzed" in figurative contexts. However, "frozen" tends to emphasize the momentary, sudden quality of being unable to move — like a rabbit caught in headlights. "Paralyzed" can suggest something more lasting or deeply rooted.

She froze when she heard the noise. → A sudden, brief halt.
She was paralyzed by the diagnosis for months. → A prolonged inability to function.

Paralyzed vs. Helpless

"Helpless" means you are unable to help yourself or change the situation. It emphasizes powerlessness over your circumstances.

"Paralyzed" emphasizes the inability to act or move, which may include being helpless — but is specifically about that frozen, non-functional state.

He felt helpless watching the situation unfold. → He could see what was happening but couldn't stop it.
He was paralyzed watching the situation unfold. → He couldn't even move or respond in any way.
The Spectrum: How "Paralyzed" Can Vary in Intensity

Even though "paralyzed" implies a total inability, the word is used across a range of intensities in practice:

  • Fully paralyzed — complete shutdown, no function whatsoever. ("The patient was fully paralyzed from the neck down.")
  • Partially paralyzed — some function remains, but a significant part is lost. ("Her left arm was partially paralyzed after the surgery.")
  • Momentarily paralyzed — frozen for a short time before recovering. ("For a second, she was paralyzed by the shock — then she ran.")
  • Effectively paralyzed — not technically paralyzed, but functioning so poorly that the result is the same. ("The committee was effectively paralyzed by endless debate.")
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Paralyzed" is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of helplessness, vulnerability, and loss of control. When you call someone paralyzed, you are communicating that they are not choosing to be inactive — something has done this to them. This makes it a word full of empathy and gravity.

This is why it's often used to describe:

  • Trauma survivors ("She was emotionally paralyzed by what she had witnessed.")
  • People in impossible situations ("He was paralyzed — no matter what he chose, someone would get hurt.")
  • Societies in crisis ("The nation was paralyzed, unsure of what the future would bring.")

Paralyzed means being in a state of complete inability to move, act, or function — either because the body's nervous system has failed to deliver signals to the muscles, or because an emotion, situation, or force has overwhelmed a person or system so thoroughly that all normal activity has stopped.
11701: A paramedic is a highly trained emergency medical professional who provides advanced medical care to patients before and during transport to a hospital. They are the skilled healthcare workers who typically arrive at the scene of a medical emergency — in an ambulance, a helicopter, or on foot — and deliver immediate, life-saving treatment right where the crisis is happening.

Think of it this way: when someone has a heart attack, suffers a serious injury in a car crash, stops breathing, or faces any sudden, life-threatening crisis — they cannot wait. Every passing minute without treatment can mean permanent damage or death. A hospital may be fifteen minutes away. Those fifteen minutes matter enormously.

This is exactly the problem a paramedic solves.

A paramedic brings advanced medical care to the patient, rather than making the patient wait to reach a hospital. They are the bridge between the moment a crisis strikes and the moment a person safely arrives in an emergency room. Their job is to keep patients alive, stable, and as well as possible during that critical window.

Paramedics are not simply people who drive ambulances or "carry patients on a stretcher." Their scope of work is genuinely medical and highly complex. Here is what they are trained and authorized to do:

Assess and diagnose on the spot. When a paramedic arrives at a scene, they quickly examine the patient — checking vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, oxygen levels), asking questions, and figuring out what is going wrong. This rapid assessment is crucial because it shapes every decision that follows.

Perform advanced life support (ALS). This is the defining characteristic of a paramedic. "Advanced life support" refers to a set of medical interventions that go far beyond basic first aid. Paramedics can:

  • Intubate — insert a breathing tube down a patient's airway to keep them breathing when they cannot do so themselves.
  • Administer medications — paramedics can give a wide range of drugs, including adrenaline (epinephrine) for cardiac arrest, morphine for severe pain, glucose for diabetic emergencies, nitroglycerine for chest pain, and many others. They inject these through IVs (directly into veins) or other routes.
  • Defibrillate — deliver an electric shock to the heart when it is in a dangerous abnormal rhythm, attempting to restore a normal heartbeat.
  • Interpret an ECG (electrocardiogram) — read the electrical activity of the heart to identify conditions like heart attacks in real time.
  • Start IV lines — insert needles into veins and administer fluids or medications directly into the bloodstream.
  • Decompress a chest — in cases of a collapsed lung, insert a needle to relieve dangerous pressure.
  • Manage trauma — treat severe bleeding, splint broken bones, immobilize the spine, and handle major injuries.

Make medical decisions independently. Paramedics work largely on their own judgment in the field, guided by established medical protocols. A doctor is not physically present with them — the paramedic must observe, decide, and act, often under enormous time pressure and in difficult environments.

Communicate with the hospital. As they work, paramedics contact the receiving hospital to give advance warning about the patient's condition, so the medical team there can be fully prepared the moment the ambulance arrives.

Transport and continue care. The paramedic does not stop working once the patient is inside the ambulance. They continue monitoring and treating the patient throughout the journey to the hospital.

Though the ambulance is the most familiar setting, paramedics work in many environments:

  • Ground ambulances — the most common setting, responding to emergency calls.
  • Air ambulances and helicopters — for patients in remote areas or when speed is critical.
  • Disaster and mass-casualty events — major accidents, building collapses, terrorist incidents, natural disasters.
  • Fire services — in many countries, paramedics are integrated into fire departments.
  • Hospital emergency departments — some paramedics work inside hospitals, especially in resuscitation rooms.
  • Sports events and concerts — large gatherings require on-site medical coverage.
  • Military and conflict zones — combat paramedics provide battlefield trauma care.
  • Community paramedicine programs — paramedics visit high-risk patients at home to prevent emergencies before they happen.
How Paramedics Differ from Similar Roles

Understanding a paramedic becomes much clearer when you compare them to related roles.

Paramedic vs. EMT (Emergency Medical Technician)

An EMT (also called an Emergency Medical Technician) is the role below a paramedic in the hierarchy of pre-hospital emergency care. This distinction is important.

EMTs provide basic life support (BLS). They can perform CPR, use a defibrillator (in its simpler automatic form), manage airways with basic tools, control bleeding, and provide oxygen. However, they cannot give most medications, cannot intubate, and cannot perform invasive procedures.

A paramedic provides advanced life support (ALS). The paramedic has significantly more training and a far broader scope of practice. They can do everything an EMT can do — and much more. The paramedic is the more senior, more clinically capable role.

In many emergency services, both an EMT and a paramedic work together on the same ambulance. The paramedic leads the clinical care; the EMT assists.

Paramedic vs. Doctor

A doctor has far more extensive education (typically 8–12+ years of training) and can diagnose and treat virtually any condition. Paramedics work within specific protocols and cannot diagnose conditions in the formal sense — they are trained to recognize and respond to specific emergencies.

However, the crucial difference in practice is where they work. Doctors typically work in controlled settings — hospitals, clinics. A paramedic works in the field, in unpredictable environments, with limited equipment, under time pressure, often alone or with a single partner. Their skill set is specifically designed for that context.

In most countries, paramedics operate under the medical authority of a supervising or medical director physician, meaning a doctor ultimately authorizes the protocols they follow — but the paramedic makes independent clinical decisions in real time.

Paramedic vs. Nurse

Nurses provide ongoing patient care, typically inside a hospital or clinic. While some nurses specialize in emergency care, and some have training that overlaps with paramedics, nurses work in clinical environments with full resources available. Paramedics work outside those environments, in the community, bringing emergency care to wherever the patient is.

Becoming a paramedic requires serious, rigorous training — it is not a basic certification course. While requirements vary by country, the path typically involves:

  • Completing a formal paramedic education program, which can range from approximately one to four years depending on the country and qualification level. In many places, this is a university degree or an advanced diploma.
  • Studying subjects including human anatomy and physiology, pharmacology (the science of drugs), pathophysiology (how diseases affect the body), patient assessment, emergency medical procedures, trauma care, cardiac care, and more.
  • Extensive hands-on clinical practice — riding along on real ambulances and working in hospital emergency departments under supervision.
  • Passing national or regional licensing examinations and background checks.
  • Maintaining ongoing training and re-certification throughout their career, as medical knowledge evolves.

Paramedics are licensed or registered professionals. They are recognized healthcare workers, not informal helpers. In many countries, using the title "paramedic" without proper certification is illegal.

Here are some natural ways you might encounter or use this word:

  • "The paramedic knelt beside the patient and began assessing his breathing and pulse."
  • "She always wanted to work in emergency medicine, so she trained to become a paramedic."
  • "The paramedic administered a dose of epinephrine during the cardiac arrest and prepared the patient for transport."
  • "There were two paramedics on the ambulance crew — one drove while the other treated the patient in the back."
  • "The air paramedic was winched down to the injured hiker on the mountainside."
  • "After the accident, witnesses called for emergency services, and paramedics arrived within eight minutes."

• Paramedics — the plural form. "The paramedics worked together to stabilize the patient."
  • Paramedical — the adjective form, meaning "relating to paramedics or the work they do," or more broadly, relating to healthcare workers who support but are not fully qualified as doctors. "She pursued a paramedical career in emergency services."
  • Paramedicine — the noun referring to the professional field or discipline of paramedic practice. "Paramedicine has evolved enormously over the past few decades."
  • EMS (Emergency Medical Services) — the broader system that paramedics are part of, which includes the coordination of ambulances, dispatch, hospitals, and emergency responders. Paramedics are a key component of EMS.

In modern healthcare, paramedics occupy a unique and vital position. They are the first medically trained eyes on a patient during the most critical moments of an emergency. In conditions like cardiac arrest, stroke, or major trauma — where every minute without treatment significantly worsens outcomes — the paramedic's skill, speed, and calm under pressure can be the difference between life and death, or between full recovery and permanent disability.

They carry a hospital's worth of core emergency capabilities in a bag and a vehicle, and they use those capabilities in parking lots, living rooms, roadsides, and disaster zones. It is demanding, physically and emotionally exhausting work — but it is also among the most directly life-saving professions that exists.
11702:
A parameter is a value, condition, or boundary that defines how something behaves or is described — without being the main thing you're studying or producing itself.

It sits in the background. It sets the stage. Change a parameter, and you change the outcome or the shape of the whole thing.

A simple way to feel this intuitively: imagine a thermostat. The temperature you set is the parameter. The actual behavior of the room — heating up, cooling down — flows from that setting. The parameter doesn't do the work; it governs how the work is done.

In ordinary conversation, "parameters" (almost always used in the plural) means the defined limits, rules, or conditions within which something must happen.

  • "Let's agree on the parameters of this project before we start." → Let's agree on the boundaries and constraints — budget, timeline, scope — before we begin.
  • "The architect had to work within the parameters set by the city." → The city imposed certain rules (maximum height, approved materials), and the architect had to stay within them.
  • "The negotiation must happen within acceptable parameters." → There are limits beyond which the deal cannot go.

So in everyday use: parameters ≈ the governing conditions or limits that define the space in which something operates.

Here the word gets more precise. In math, a parameter is a quantity that is fixed for a specific situation but that you can adjust to describe a different situation. It defines which particular version of something you're looking at.

To understand this, it helps to compare three types of quantities:

Variables — these change within a single situation. In the equation y = x², both x and y are variables: as x changes, y changes.

Constants — these never change, ever. The number π (pi) is always 3.14159... It is not a parameter; it is a fixed truth of the universe.

Parameters — these are fixed for a given situation, but you get to choose them, and different choices give you a different situation entirely.

Example: the equation of a straight line is y = mx + b.

  • x and y are variables — they move around as you trace the line.
  • m (the slope — how steep the line is) and b (where the line crosses the vertical axis) are parameters — they are fixed for this particular line, but by changing them you can describe any straight line in existence.

So the parameters m and b define which line you're talking about. They don't vary during the situation; they describe the situation.

This idea extends to science. In a physics experiment, things like temperature, pressure, or mass are often parameters — you fix them for a given experiment, but you can change them to design a different experiment and study how the outcome shifts.

In statistics, "parameter" has a very specific meaning: a true, fixed characteristic of an entire population.

Suppose you want to know the average salary of every working adult in a country. That true average — one single number that exists in reality — is a parameter. It is fixed and real, but the problem is you usually cannot measure it directly, because you can't collect data from every single person.

So instead, you take a sample (a smaller group), calculate the average from that sample, and use it to estimate the true parameter. The number you get from the sample is called a statistic (not a parameter).

The essential distinction:

  • Parameter = a truth about the whole population (often unknown; you try to estimate it)
  • Statistic = a fact calculated from a sample (used to approximate the parameter)

In programming, a parameter is a named placeholder inside a function definition — a slot waiting to be filled with a real value.

Imagine you write a function called "send_greeting" that greets someone by name. When you define that function, you write a placeholder — say, "name" — so the function knows a name is going to come in. That placeholder is the parameter.

When someone actually uses (calls) that function, they supply a real value — "Alice," "Bob," or whatever. That real value supplied at the moment of use is technically called an argument.

So:

  • Parameter = the placeholder slot you define when writing the function ("name")
  • Argument = the actual value you put in when using the function ("Alice")

In everyday programming talk, people often use these two words interchangeably, and that is fine in casual conversation. But strictly speaking, they are different: parameter is the slot, argument is what fills it.
In Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning

This context is increasingly important today. When you hear that an AI model has "billions of parameters," it means the model contains billions of internal numerical values — learned during training — that together determine how the model processes an input and produces an output.

Each parameter is essentially a tiny dial. During training, the AI adjusts all these dials millions of times to get better at its task. Once training is done, those dials are set, and the collection of all their values is what defines that specific model's "knowledge" and behavior. A model with more parameters is generally capable of capturing more complexity — which is why parameter count is often used as a rough measure of a model's size and capacity.
An Important Distinction: Parameter vs. Variable

A very common point of confusion is when to call something a parameter versus a variable. Here is the cleanest way to think about it:

A variable changes during the situation you're analyzing. A parameter is held constant during the situation, but it's what you adjust between situations.

If you're studying how a ball rolls down a hill, the ball's position and speed at each moment are variables — they change as the ball moves. The steepness of the hill and the weight of the ball are parameters — they are fixed during this one roll, but if you set up a new experiment with a steeper hill, you've changed the parameter.

The same quantity can be a variable or a parameter depending on your perspective. If you're asking "how does this system behave right now?" — you're treating certain things as parameters. If you're asking "how does this system behave as this value changes?" — you may be treating that same thing as a variable.

These two words look visually similar, which causes frequent mix-ups — but they mean entirely different things and are unrelated.

Perimeter is a geometry term. It means the total length of the outer boundary of a shape. The perimeter of a square with sides of 5 cm is 20 cm.

Parameter has nothing to do with the edge of a shape. It is about defining values, governing conditions, or constraining boundaries in a broader, more abstract sense.

If you're talking about a shape's outline, it's perimeter. In virtually every other context — math, science, computing, everyday language — it's parameter.

Across every context, what makes something a "parameter" is this:

It is not the main thing you are directly studying or producing. It is a background value that defines the conditions under which the main thing happens. It shapes the system. Change it, and the system behaves differently.

Whether it's the slope of a line, the rules of a project, a placeholder in code, or a dial inside an AI model — a parameter is always the thing that defines the nature of the situation, not the situation's output itself.
11703:
Paramount means more important than everything else. Not just very important — but the most important, sitting above all other concerns. When something is paramount, nothing outranks it. It holds the highest position on the scale of importance, and everything else comes second to it.

Think of it this way: if you have a list of ten priorities, something "important" could sit anywhere on that list. Something paramount is always #1 — and not merely #1 by a small margin, but so decisively at the top that nothing else even competes with it.

This is the most important thing to understand about "paramount": the word is already superlative by nature. It means the highest. This is why you would not normally say "more paramount" or "most paramount" — that would be like saying "more unique" or "more perfect." The word already carries the meaning of the maximum. You can't go beyond it.

So when someone calls something paramount, they are making a very strong, definitive statement. They are saying: this, above all other things.
What It Implies in a Sentence

When you call something paramount, you are silently communicating two things at once:

  1. This is the top priority. It ranks above everything else.
  2. This is non-negotiable. Because it sits at the top, it cannot be sacrificed or traded away for something else.

For example: "In a hospital, patient safety is paramount."

This doesn't just mean patient safety is important. It means: if there is ever a conflict between patient safety and any other concern — cost, convenience, speed, anything — patient safety wins. Always. No debate.

• "The safety of the children is paramount."

Everything else — budget, schedules, rules — is secondary. Nothing overrides the children's safety.

  • "In this negotiation, trust is paramount."

Without trust, nothing else in the negotiation even matters. It is the foundation on which everything else rests, and it is the most important element.

  • "For a surgeon, steady hands and focus are paramount."

These qualities matter more than any other skill or trait a surgeon could have.

  • "During a crisis, clear communication is paramount."

You might be able to overlook other shortcomings during a crisis, but if communication breaks down, everything falls apart. It is the one thing that cannot slip.

Notice a pattern in all these examples: something paramount is usually the thing that, if lost or ignored, makes everything else irrelevant or impossible.
The Most Common Phrase: "Of Paramount Importance"

You will very frequently encounter the fixed phrase "of paramount importance." This is simply a formal, emphatic way of saying something is the most important thing. It appears often in professional, legal, academic, and official writing.

"It is of paramount importance that all documents are submitted before the deadline." → Submitting documents on time matters more than anything else in this situation.

"Paramount" is a formal word. You would use it in serious, professional, or official contexts — safety briefings, policy documents, business strategy, medical settings, legal discussions. You would not use it in casual conversation. Saying "Pizza tonight is paramount" would sound strange and out of place. The word carries weight and gravity, so it signals to the listener or reader: pay close attention, this is serious.

Many words are close to "paramount" in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavour:

  • Important — broad and general. Many things can be important at the same time. "Paramount" is reserved for the single thing that tops them all.
  • Critical / Crucial — these words emphasize urgency and risk. Something critical often implies that failure has serious consequences. "Paramount" is more about rank and priority than urgency.
  • Primary / Main — these mean first among several things. The "primary goal" is the main goal, but other goals still exist alongside it. "Paramount" is more absolute — it suggests everything else bows to it.
  • Supreme — very close to "paramount." But "supreme" often relates to rank, quality, or authority (the Supreme Court, supreme leader). "Paramount" is more specifically about importance and priority.

The simplest way to remember the difference: use "paramount" when you want to say something is #1 above all else, with no contest.

• It does not mean good or excellent. A paramount concern could be a problem — something of paramount concern could be a serious threat, not a positive thing.
  • It does not mean urgent on its own, though something paramount is often treated urgently.
  • It has nothing to do with size, quantity, or quality of an object — it is purely about rank and importance.
A Simple Mental Image to Remember It

Picture a mountain. At the very top — the peak — sits the most important thing. That thing at the peak is paramount. Everything else is lower down the mountain. No matter how high the other things are, they are still below the peak. The paramount thing is always, always at the summit.
Paramount means: more important than everything else, sitting at the top of all priorities with nothing above it.
11704:
A paramour is a person's secret romantic or sexual partner — someone they are involved with outside of their marriage or committed relationship. In the simplest terms, a paramour is the person someone is having an affair with.

Think of it this way: if a married person falls in love with someone who is not their spouse, and they carry on a hidden romantic relationship with that person, that hidden partner is their paramour.
The Key Ideas Packed Into This Word

The word "paramour" is not just a fancy word for "girlfriend" or "boyfriend." It carries specific meaning. There are a few things always implied when this word is used:

1. There is an existing, official relationship being betrayed.
A paramour exists because someone is already in a marriage or a serious, committed partnership. Without that primary relationship, the word doesn't quite apply. The paramour is, by nature, the other person — the one on the side.

2. The relationship is secret or forbidden.
A paramour is not someone you bring to family dinners or introduce to friends openly. The relationship is hidden, often shameful in the eyes of society, and carried out discreetly. There is always a sense of something illicit — something that violates a promise or social expectation.

3. It implies genuine romantic or emotional depth, not just a casual encounter.
A paramour is not just a one-night stand. The word implies an ongoing connection — one that has some emotional or romantic weight to it. It is a relationship, even if a secret one.

A paramour can be any gender. A woman can be a man's paramour. A man can be a woman's paramour. Unlike the word "mistress" — which refers specifically to a woman who is the secret lover of a married man — "paramour" is completely gender-neutral, which makes it a broader and more flexible word.
What Tone Does This Word Carry?

"Paramour" is a formal and literary word. It has a slightly old-fashioned, even poetic feel to it. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Classic and modern literature (novels, poetry, plays)
  • Journalism and formal writing (especially when reporting on scandals)
  • Historical writing (it was widely used in earlier centuries)

In everyday casual conversation, people rarely say "paramour." They are more likely to say "affair partner," "secret lover," or just "the person they were seeing on the side." But when a writer or journalist does use "paramour," it immediately signals a relationship that is illicit and romantic — and it does so with elegance and precision.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are some examples to see the word in action:

  • "The king's paramour was a noblewoman from the south, whose identity was an open secret at court."
  • "When the letters were discovered, the truth about her paramour came to light."
  • "He had kept his paramour hidden from his family for three years."
  • "The scandal broke when the senator's paramour spoke to the press."

In each of these, you can feel the secrecy, the romance, and the forbidden nature of the relationship.

It helps to see how this word sits alongside related words:

  • Lover — A "lover" simply means someone you have a romantic or sexual relationship with. It does not automatically imply that anyone is cheating or that there is an existing relationship being betrayed. A paramour is always a type of lover, but not every lover is a paramour.
  • Mistress — A "mistress" refers specifically to a woman who is the secret lover of a man who is already married or committed. "Paramour" covers the same idea but applies to any gender.
  • Spouse / Partner — These are the official, public, recognized relationships. The paramour is the opposite of this — hidden, unofficial, and existing in the shadows of the official relationship.
One Sentence to Remember It By

If you ever want to recall what "paramour" means in a flash, remember this:

A paramour is the secret lover someone keeps while they are already committed to someone else.

Everything else about the word — its formality, its suggestion of ongoing romance, its gender-neutrality — flows naturally from that core idea.
11705:
Paranoia is a state of mind in which a person has strong feelings of suspicion, distrust, or fear — believing that others are out to harm, deceive, or persecute them — even when there is little or no real reason to believe so.

The single most important thing to understand about paranoia is that the belief feels completely real and true to the person experiencing it, even though it is either false, greatly exaggerated, or a serious misreading of reality.

Think of it this way. Imagine you walk into a room and two people stop talking. A normal reaction might be, "Oh, maybe they were having a private conversation." A paranoid reaction would be, "They were definitely talking about me. They are plotting against me. I can't trust anyone here."

The paranoid person doesn't just wonder — they become convinced. And that conviction is not backed by solid evidence. That gap — between what is real and what the person believes — is where paranoia lives.

Paranoia exists on a spectrum, from everyday feelings to a serious clinical condition.

1. Everyday paranoia (mild and common)

Most people experience a mild, passing form of paranoia at some point in their lives. This is the informal, everyday use of the word.

  • Feeling like your friends are ignoring you on purpose when they're just busy.
  • Thinking a colleague is trying to make you look bad at work, with no real proof.
  • Believing people are staring at you and judging you when you walk into a room.

This kind of paranoia is usually temporary. It fades when you calm down, think clearly, or get more information. Stress, anxiety, lack of sleep, and social pressure can all trigger this level of paranoia in ordinary people.

2. Clinical paranoia (severe and persistent)

At its more serious end, paranoia is a psychiatric symptom — a deep, fixed, unshakeable false belief that others are working against you. Doctors call such a belief a delusion.

At this level, the person might believe:

  • That the government is spying on them specifically.
  • That their food is being poisoned by someone close to them.
  • That strangers on the street are secretly following them.

No amount of reassurance, logic, or evidence changes their mind. The belief is locked in place. This level of paranoia appears in serious mental health conditions such as paranoid schizophrenia and paranoid personality disorder, and it requires professional medical help.

No matter the level, paranoia always involves these core features:

Unfounded or exaggerated suspicion. The fear or distrust is either completely baseless or wildly out of proportion to what is actually happening.

A focus on being targeted. Paranoia almost always revolves around the idea that you specifically are being watched, harmed, cheated, or plotted against. It is deeply personal.

A feeling of certainty. The paranoid person doesn't say, "I think maybe..." — they feel sure. This is what makes paranoia different from ordinary worry or doubt.

Difficulty being reasoned with. Because the belief feels so real, logic and evidence have little power over it. Trying to convince a paranoid person that they are wrong often makes them more suspicious — even of the person trying to help.
What paranoia is NOT — important distinctions

Paranoia is not the same as caution or healthy skepticism.
Being careful, questioning people's motives with good reason, or protecting yourself from real risks is not paranoia. Paranoia is specifically about suspicion that goes beyond what the evidence justifies.

Paranoia is not the same as justified fear.
If someone is genuinely following you, and you are afraid of them, that is not paranoia — that is a reasonable response to a real threat. Paranoia only applies when the threat is imagined or greatly blown out of proportion.

Paranoia is not always a mental illness.
Feeling paranoid in a stressful situation is a normal human experience. The word is used both casually (to describe a passing feeling) and clinically (to describe a serious symptom). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
How paranoia is used in sentences

• "She was filled with paranoia after receiving anonymous messages, convinced someone was out to ruin her career."
  • "A little paranoia is normal when you're new to a job and still figuring out who you can trust."
  • "His paranoia had reached a point where he believed his own family was spying on him — a clear sign he needed medical help."
  • "The constant paranoia exhausted him; he could never relax, always expecting the worst from people."

• Paranoid (adjective): describing a person or state affected by paranoia. "She felt paranoid all day."
  • Paranoid (adjective, clinical): used in medical diagnoses, such as paranoid schizophrenia or paranoid personality disorder.
  • Paranoiac (noun): a formal or clinical word for a person who suffers from paranoia.
The essence of the word, in one sentence

Paranoia is an unwarranted and often unshakeable belief that the world — or specific people in it — is threatening, deceiving, or conspiring against you, even when reality does not support that belief.
11706:
A paranoiac is a person whose mind is held in a persistent grip of irrational suspicion — someone who is deeply, unshakeably convinced that others are out to harm them, deceive them, watch them, or conspire against them, even when there is no real evidence for this.

The single most important word in understanding a paranoiac is irrational. This is not ordinary caution. This is not reasonable wariness based on past experience. A paranoiac's suspicions are disconnected from reality — yet to the paranoiac, those suspicions feel completely and absolutely real. You cannot talk them out of it. You cannot show them evidence to the contrary. Their belief stands firm.

A paranoiac's mind takes neutral, innocent events and twists them into signs of threat. A coworker who glances their way is "spying on me." A neighbor's friendly wave is "a mask for their true intentions." A friend who doesn't reply to a message immediately has "turned against me." To an outside observer, these interpretations seem wildly out of proportion. To the paranoiac, they are cold, hard facts.

Over time, many paranoiacs develop what are called delusions — fixed, false beliefs that they hold with complete certainty, no matter how much evidence or reason is placed in front of them. Common examples:

  • A secret organization is tracking their every move.
  • The government has been tapping their phone and reading their mail for years.
  • Their colleagues have formed a hidden alliance to sabotage their career.
  • Strangers they have never met are conspiring to ruin their life.

These beliefs do not waver. They are not "fears" the paranoiac entertains and then dismisses — they are what the paranoiac knows to be true.
The paranoiac vs. an anxious or cautious person

This distinction matters, because people often use "paranoid" loosely in everyday speech.

A cautious person is wary for rational reasons — they have been burned before, or they see real warning signs. Their guard is proportionate and evidence-based.

An anxious person worries excessively and often without good reason, but they can — at least sometimes — recognize that their fears might be exaggerated. They might say, "I know I'm probably overreacting."

A paranoiac does neither of these things. They do not recognize any possibility that they might be wrong. Their suspicion is not a feeling they question — it is a certainty they defend. That inability to doubt their own beliefs is what sets a paranoiac apart.

When someone says casually, "I'm just being paranoid," they are using the word loosely. A true paranoiac would never say that — because they don't think they're being paranoid at all. They think they're simply seeing the world clearly.
The two main flavors of paranoid thinking

Persecutory paranoia is the most common type. The paranoiac believes others are working against them — persecuting, plotting, surveilling, or harming them. ("They are all against me. They want to destroy me.") This is the classic image most people have of a paranoiac.

Grandiose paranoia is less common but real. Here, the paranoiac believes they are a uniquely special, chosen, or important person — and that powerful forces are envious of them or trying to prevent them from fulfilling their special mission. The suspicion still runs through it, but it is wrapped in a sense of self-importance rather than pure victimhood.

In psychiatry and psychology, "paranoiac" refers to a person with a recognized condition. There are several:

Paranoid personality disorder — The person has a deep, lifelong pattern of extreme suspicion and distrust as a core feature of their personality. They are perpetually guarded, read hidden threatening meanings into ordinary remarks, and hold grudges for a very long time. Crucially, they have not lost touch with reality in the way someone with psychosis has — they do not hear voices or have full-blown delusions. But their world is colored so completely by distrust that normal relationships become nearly impossible.

Delusional disorder (paranoid type) — The person holds one or more specific, firm delusions — most commonly of a persecutory nature — but is otherwise functioning relatively normally. They may hold a job, maintain relationships, and appear ordinary in most ways, while privately believing, say, that their neighbor is poisoning their food supply.

Paranoid schizophrenia — Here, paranoid delusions combine with the broader symptoms of schizophrenia, including hallucinations (most commonly hearing voices), disorganized thinking, and a breakdown in the person's ability to function. The paranoiac in this case does not just believe others are against them — they may hear those persecutors speaking to them.

All three involve the core feature: persistent, irrational, unshakeable suspicion of others.
How a paranoiac lives day to day

Because a paranoiac cannot trust anyone, their daily existence is exhausting and deeply isolating.

They are constantly on guard — scanning their environment for threats, reading between the lines of every conversation, second-guessing every act of kindness (which they often interpret as manipulation). Sharing information feels dangerous. Vulnerability feels fatal.

Relationships crumble. Friends and family, no matter how loyal, eventually fall under suspicion too. The paranoiac may slowly cut off the people closest to them — and then interpret this growing isolation as further proof that the world has turned against them. It becomes a self-reinforcing cycle.

There is often tremendous inner suffering. The world, as a paranoiac experiences it, is a hostile place full of hidden enemies. That is an exhausting and frightening way to live — and the tragedy is that the paranoiac believes this is simply the reality everyone else refuses to see.

• "He refused to discuss his plans on any phone or in any email — the paranoiac was certain every line was being monitored."
  • "Even when presented with evidence that no one was following her, the paranoiac remained unmoved; the proof itself, she said, was part of the cover-up."
  • "His family watched helplessly as the paranoiac slowly severed every relationship, convinced that each person had secretly betrayed him."
The short version, if you need it

A paranoiac is a person with an irrational, unshakeable conviction that others are against them — watching them, plotting against them, or trying to harm them — with no sufficient evidence to support this belief, and no ability to be reasoned out of it.
11707:
When you describe someone as paranoid, you mean that person believes — without any real, solid evidence — that others are secretly out to get them, are watching them, are plotting against them, or are trying to harm them in some way.

The critical idea is that the threat they believe in is either completely imaginary, or wildly exaggerated beyond what the situation actually warrants.

Being paranoid isn't just a cold, logical thought. It is a feeling — and a very uncomfortable one. A paranoid person genuinely feels unsafe, watched, targeted, or persecuted. That feeling is completely real to them, even if there is no real danger outside their mind. They are not pretending or lying. Their mind has, in a sense, convinced itself that threats exist where there are none.

Imagine walking into a room and immediately feeling certain that everyone just stopped talking because they were talking about you — and that they're all against you. That nagging, unsettled, suspicious feeling is the essence of what it means to be paranoid.
The most important distinction: paranoid vs. justified concern

This is the crucial point to understand the word properly.

Being paranoid is not the same as being rightfully cautious or worried.

  • If someone is genuinely following you on the street, being scared is not paranoid — it's rational.
  • If your employer has actually been reading your private messages, being upset about it is not paranoid — it's a reasonable reaction to a real situation.

Paranoia is specifically when the fear or suspicion has no solid basis in reality, or when it is massively disproportionate to any actual evidence. The moment real, reasonable evidence supports the concern, it is no longer paranoia.

This distinction is what makes the word meaningful. Calling someone paranoid when they have real reasons for their worry is inaccurate — and, frankly, dismissive.

In everyday conversation, people use "paranoid" quite loosely — often in a light, self-aware, even slightly humorous way — to describe ordinary overthinking or excessive suspicion, especially about what others might think or do.

  • "I sent the email and now I keep re-reading it to check if I accidentally said something rude. I'm being so paranoid."
  • "Every time my boss doesn't reply quickly, I get paranoid that she's angry with me."
  • "I'm sure someone moved my bag — or maybe I'm just being paranoid."
  • "Don't be paranoid — they're not talking about you."

In this casual sense, the person often recognizes, at least partly, that they are probably overreacting. They use the word almost self-critically, to acknowledge that their suspicion is likely unfounded.

In psychology and psychiatry, paranoid has a more precise and serious meaning. It describes a persistent, deep-seated pattern of suspicion and distrust that significantly disrupts a person's life. This is not occasional, mild overthinking — it is an ongoing mental state that the person cannot easily shake off, even when given clear evidence that their fears are unfounded.

Paranoid personality disorder is a condition where a person persistently suspects others — including friends, family, and colleagues — of lying to them, exploiting them, or working to harm them, despite having no real evidence. They find it almost impossible to trust anyone. They may read innocent actions as hostile. A friend who cancels plans might be seen as deliberately avoiding them. A colleague who offers feedback might be seen as trying to sabotage them.

Paranoid schizophrenia is a more severe condition where a person may experience delusions — which are fixed, false beliefs that feel absolutely real to them. For example, they might genuinely believe that the government has planted a listening device in their home, that strangers on the street are secret agents sent to monitor them, or that they are being controlled by some external force. These beliefs feel as real to the person as any ordinary fact of life, which is what makes the condition so difficult and distressing.

In clinical settings, what makes paranoia especially serious is that the person typically cannot be reasoned out of their beliefs. Even when shown clear, concrete evidence to the contrary, they may still be fully convinced the threat is real. They might interpret the counter-evidence itself as part of the conspiracy.

Paranoia is not an either/or thing — it ranges from mild to severe, and people can sit anywhere on that range.

Mild: "I know my friends probably aren't talking behind my back, but I can't shake the feeling that they are." — The person doubts their own suspicion. They recognize it is likely unfounded.

Moderate: "I'm completely sure my coworkers are scheming to make me look bad and get me fired." — The person is more convinced. They're not laughing it off. It affects their behavior at work.

Severe: Firmly believing one is being tracked by satellites, that strangers are agents of a secret organization, or that a family member is slowly poisoning their food. The person is fully convinced and sees no reason to doubt it.

The milder forms are something many people experience briefly — during stressful periods, after being betrayed, or in moments of insecurity. The severe forms are symptoms of serious mental illness that require professional care.
What can be described as paranoid?

The word applies to more than just people. You can describe:

  • A person: "He's quite paranoid — he thinks everyone at the office is working against him."
  • A thought: "I know this is a paranoid thought, but I keep feeling like my neighbor is monitoring me."
  • A feeling: "That paranoid feeling crept in every time someone whispered nearby."
  • A reaction or response: "Changing your locks because your friend borrowed your pen is a paranoid reaction."
  • A state of mind: "After years of betrayal, she lived in a constant paranoid state."
  • A style of thinking: "The group had a paranoid worldview — they believed every institution was corrupt and secretly targeting ordinary people."

Not the same as general anxiety. Anxiety is a broad, wide-ranging feeling of worry or unease — it can be about anything: health, money, the future. Paranoia is more specific. It involves the suspicion that other people or forces are deliberately working against you. You can be anxious without being paranoid.

Not the same as caution. A careful, vigilant person who locks their door, checks their bank statement regularly, or avoids sharing sensitive information online is not paranoid — they are sensible. Paranoia involves fear that is disconnected from reasonable evidence.

Not a word for valid, evidence-based concern. If someone has real reasons to be suspicious — a history of being genuinely deceived, actual evidence of wrongdoing, or a legitimately dangerous situation — calling them paranoid would be unfair and wrong.

Paranoid describes a state of mind in which a person believes, without sufficient justification, that they are being targeted, watched, deceived, or harmed by others. The belief feels very real to the person holding it, but it is not grounded in solid evidence.

In casual speech, it often means excessive, unfounded suspicion or overthinking — used lightly and self-awarely.

In clinical settings, it means a serious, persistent pattern of distrust and fear that can significantly affect a person's life and relationships, and that resists correction even when contradicted by evidence.

The word lives comfortably in both worlds, and context will almost always tell you which sense is meant.
11708: When we describe something as paranormal, we are saying it falls beyond the reach of what science can currently explain or confirm. Think of "normal" as everything the natural world accounts for — gravity pulling things downward, fire producing heat, the heart pumping blood — phenomena that science can consistently measure, test, and explain. The paranormal is the space just past that boundary, where things appear to happen but defy those well-established rules entirely.

As an adjective, "paranormal" modifies nouns — it stamps them with the label of "scientifically unexplained." You will most commonly encounter it paired with words like: paranormal activity, paranormal phenomena, paranormal event, paranormal experience, paranormal investigation, and paranormal claim. Every time you see it, it signals that whatever follows cannot be neatly accounted for by ordinary science or nature.
The Kinds of Things It Covers

The paranormal is a wide and varied category. Ghosts and hauntings — the supposed lingering presence of the souls of the dead — are perhaps the most classic example. Telepathy (the claimed ability to read another person's mind), telekinesis (supposedly moving objects using only the power of thought), precognition (appearing to know future events before they occur), communication with the dead, poltergeists (invisible forces that reportedly hurl or move objects on their own), psychic abilities, and out-of-body experiences all fall under this umbrella. The single thread connecting all of them is that no scientific experiment has ever been able to reliably prove, reproduce, or explain them under controlled conditions.
A Very Important Nuance: Neutral on Reality

This is something many people miss. The word "paranormal" does not take a side. It does not claim these things are definitely real, and it does not claim they are definitely fake. It simply labels them as falling outside what mainstream science can explain. A scientist investigating a haunted house might say, "There is no credible evidence supporting these paranormal claims" — using the word with healthy skepticism. A believer in the same house might say, "I felt a paranormal presence in that room" — using the exact same word with complete sincerity. The word carries both uses comfortably. It is a label for the unexplained, not a verdict on the truth.

You will sometimes hear "paranormal" and "supernatural" used interchangeably, but they carry a slightly different flavor. Supernatural is the older, more traditionally religious word — it typically points to things like God, miracles, angels, demons, or divine intervention, things rooted in spiritual or religious belief systems. Paranormal, on the other hand, is more modern and secular. It frames unexplained events almost like unsolved puzzles — things that might have a natural explanation we just haven't found yet. It belongs more to the world of ghost hunters, psychic researchers, and mystery investigators than to theology. Think of "supernatural" as the priest's word and "paranormal" as the investigator's word, even if they sometimes describe the same thing.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Paranormal" reliably carries a sense of mystery, the unknown, unease, and sometimes outright fear. When someone says "something paranormal happened," they are communicating that an event occurred that shook their understanding of how reality is supposed to work — something deeply strange that left them without a rational explanation. In popular culture, the word is widely used in horror movies, ghost-hunting television shows, and mystery fiction, which is why it often carries a slightly eerie or thrilling atmosphere.

"Paranormal" is a strong descriptor — far stronger than words like "unusual," "strange," or "rare." A rare species of insect is not paranormal. An insect that reportedly walks through a solid wall and vanishes would be. The word sets the bar very high: it is reserved specifically for things that challenge the fundamental rules of nature as science understands them, not merely for things that are surprising or uncommon.

To tie it all together, here is how "paranormal" sounds naturally in sentences:

  • "The family reported paranormal activity in their basement — doors opening on their own and lights flickering with no electrical cause."
  • "She became interested in paranormal investigation after she heard strange sounds in her childhood home that no one could explain."
  • "Many scientists dismiss paranormal phenomena as misinterpretations of ordinary events."
  • "The film tells the story of a detective who refuses to believe in anything paranormal, until something inexplicable forces him to reconsider."
  • "He claimed to have had a paranormal experience during his surgery — floating above his own body and watching the doctors work."

In every case, "paranormal" is doing the same job: telling you that what is being described sits in that strange, shadowy territory beyond the world science has successfully mapped.
11709:
A parapet is a low, protective wall or barrier built along the edge of something elevated — such as a roof, a bridge, a balcony, a terrace, or a military fortification — to either stop people from falling off or to shield them from danger.

Think of it this way: whenever you stand on something high and there's a short wall running along the very edge to protect you, that short wall is a parapet.
The Two Main Worlds Where This Word Lives

1. Architecture and Everyday Structures

In everyday life, a parapet is the low wall you'll find at the edge of:

  • A rooftop — instead of the roof just ending with a drop, a short wall lines the edge.
  • A bridge — the low walls running along both sides of a bridge so people don't fall into the water below.
  • A balcony or terrace — sometimes, instead of a railing made of metal or glass, a solid low wall of stone or concrete is built around the edges. That's a parapet.
  • A dam — the raised wall along the top edge of a dam structure.

Its job here is straightforward: safety. It acts as a barrier between you and a dangerous drop. It is not meant to be a full wall that blocks your view entirely — it's deliberately kept low, usually around waist to chest height. You can lean over it and look down; it just stops you from accidentally tumbling over.

2. Military Fortifications

This is where the word is perhaps most historically famous. In castles, forts, and war trenches, a parapet is a low wall built at the front edge of a defensive position to protect soldiers from enemy fire, arrows, or attack.

Imagine soldiers defending a castle. They stand behind the parapet — crouching below its top edge, safe from arrows flying at them. When they need to shoot back, they briefly rise, fire, and duck back down behind it. The parapet is their shield.

In World War I trench warfare, this was extremely literal. Soldiers dug long trenches in the ground, and the earth piled up at the front edge of the trench formed a parapet — a dirt wall they hid behind. Rising above it meant exposing yourself to enemy gunfire. It was genuinely dangerous to show your head above the parapet.
The Essential Characteristics of a Parapet

Understanding these qualities will help you recognize a parapet anywhere and distinguish it from other structures:

It is always low. A parapet is never a full-height wall. If the wall goes from floor to ceiling and fully encloses a space, it's just a wall. A parapet is intentionally short — high enough to provide protection, but low enough that you can see over it or shoot over it.

It always runs along an edge. A parapet is never in the middle of a space. It sits right at the margin or boundary of something — the very edge of a bridge, the rim of a rooftop, the front line of a fortification.

It is always on or part of something elevated. You won't find a parapet on flat ground. It exists because there's a drop, a danger, or an exposed position on the other side.

It is always protective. Whether it's protecting you from a fall or from enemy fire, its defining purpose is to act as a defensive barrier.
How a Parapet Differs from Similar Things

A parapet vs. a railing: A railing (like a metal handrail on a balcony) serves a similar safety purpose but is open — you can see through the gaps. A parapet is a solid, continuous wall of stone, brick, concrete, or earth. No gaps (unless specifically designed with them — see battlements below).

A parapet vs. a full wall: A wall can be any height and encloses or separates spaces. A parapet is specifically a short wall placed at an edge for protection.

A parapet vs. a battlement: A battlement is a specific type of parapet — one that has alternating raised sections and gaps cut into the top, like the jagged crown you see on top of a castle. Those raised solid sections are called merlons, and the gaps between them are called crenels (hence the word "crenellated," meaning having a battlement). Soldiers could shelter behind the merlons and fire through the crenels. So: all battlements are parapets, but not all parapets are battlements. A simple, flat-topped low wall with no gaps is also a parapet.

The word "parapet" has also entered everyday speech as a metaphor, especially in the phrase:

"Sticking your head above the parapet" (or "raising your head above the parapet")

This idiom comes directly from the military meaning. Remember how it was dangerous for a soldier to show their head above the parapet in a trench? The phrase now means to say or do something that draws attention to yourself when doing so involves risk — risk of criticism, controversy, or backlash.

For example: "No one in the meeting wanted to stick their head above the parapet and challenge the boss's plan."

It paints a vivid picture: most people stay safely hidden, but someone brave (or reckless) rises above the protective barrier and makes themselves a target.
Quick Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture a medieval castle. You're looking at it from outside. Right at the very top of the castle walls, there's a low wall running all around the edge. Soldiers can walk along the top of the main wall and crouch behind that short wall for cover. That short wall is the parapet. Now carry that image to a modern rooftop in a city — the short wall running along the edge of the building is the exact same thing, just serving a safety purpose instead of a military one.

One sentence to remember it: A parapet is a low, solid, protective wall built along the exposed edge of any elevated structure, whether to stop you from falling or to shield you from harm.
